nodes.name: Proof of Odd-degree extensions can be ordered
nodes.statement: Since $\ch R=0$, we can apply the primitive element theorem. Let $K=F(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha\in K$, and let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$. Then $\deg f=[K:F]$ is odd. By Theorem \ref{thm:ext_ord_cond}, we need to show that the congruence \[\sum_ia_ig_i^2\equiv-1\bmod f\tag{$\star$}\] fails to hold for any non-negative $a_i\in F$ and polynomials $g_i\in F[X]$ each of degree at most $\deg f-1$. Proceed by induction on $\deg f$; if $\deg f=1$, then ($\star$) reduces to an equality of a non-negative element of $F$ with a negative one. Otherwise, suppose for a contradiction that ($\star$) holds. Without loss of generality, we may assume, for all $i$, we have $a_i\neq0$ and that $\deg g_i<\deg f$. Rearranging ($\star$), we have $\sum_ia_ig_i^2+1=hf$ for some $h\in F[X]$. Let $d=\max_i\deg g_i$; note that $d<\deg f$ by construction. Since each $a_i$ is positive, the $2d$th coefficient on the left-hand side must be positive. Therefore \[\deg h+\deg f=\deg\left(\sum_ia_ig_i^2+1\right)=2d.\] Then $\deg h$ is odd, so $h$ has an odd-degree irreducible factor $\tilde h$. We have \[\deg\tilde h\leq\deg h=2d-\deg f<\deg f,\] but $\sum_ia_ig_i^2\equiv-1\bmod\tilde h$. We are done by induction.$_\#$

nodes.statement: Let $K/R$ be an odd-degree extension of $R$. By the primitive element theorem, $K=R(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha\in K$. Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$. nodes.name: Proof of Fundamental theorem of algebra (real closed fields)
nodes.statement: By separability, every finite extension of $R$ is contained in a finite Galois extension. Since $R(i)/R$ has no intermediate fields, it suffices to show the result for finite Galois extensions. Let $K/R$ be a nontrivial Galois extension of degree $2^k\cdot a$, where $k\geq 0$ and $a\geq1$ is odd. Applying the Galois correspondence to a Sylow 2-subgroup of $\Gal(K/R)$ yields an intermediate extension of degree $a$; by Lemma \ref{lem:alg_ext_odd_deg}, we have $a=1$ (and $k>0$). If $k>1$, iterating the last construction yields intermediate extensions $K/L/M/R$ with $[L:M]=[M:R]=2$. By Lemma \ref{lem:ext_deg_2}, $M\cong R(i)$, contradicting Lemma \ref{lem:Ri_ext_deg_2}.$_\#$ Therefore $k=1$ and (by Lemma \ref{lem:ext_deg_2}) $K\cong R(i)$.
nodes.statement_short: Galois theory: a Sylow 2-subgroup and Lemma on odd extensions force degree a power of 2. Then a degree-4 tower contradicts R(i) having no quadratic extension.

nodes.name: Proof of Converse of the fundamental theorem of algebra
nodes.statement: Since $R(i)$ has no quadratic extensions, we can apply Lemma \ref{lem:sumsq_is_sq}: sums of squares in $R$ are squares in $R$, and $R$ is real. Take a non-square $a\in R$; then $R(\sqrt{a})\cong R(i)$. Suppose $i$ maps to $x+y\sqrt{a}$ for some $x,y\in R$. Then $-1=x^2+ay^2+2xy\sqrt{a}$; comparing coefficients, we get $-1=x^2+ay^2$. Since $-1$ is not a square, $y$ must be nonzero, and so $-a=(x/y)^2+(1/y)^2$ is a square. Now, fix a nonlinear odd-degree polynomial $f\in R[X]$. Then $R[X]/(f)$ cannot be a field since $R$ has no nontrivial odd-degree extensions, and so $f$ must be reducible. We are done by induction on the degree.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the three real-closed axioms: realness via the sums-of-squares lemma, squares via the isomorphism $R(\sqrt a)\cong R(i)$, roots of odd polynomials by induction.

nodes.name: Proof of Irreducible polynomials over a real closed field
nodes.statement: Let $f\in R[X]$ be monic and irreducible. The field $R_f=R[X]/(f)$ is a finite extension of $R$, so it is classified by Theorem \ref{thm:FTAlg}. If $R_f\cong R$, then $\deg f=1$, so $f=X-c$ for some $c\in R$. If $R_f\cong R(i)$, let the isomorphism be $\varphi$, and suppose $\varphi(X+(f))=a+bi$ ($a,b\in R$). Note that $b\neq0$ since $\varphi^{-1}$ is constant on $R$. Rearranging, we see that $\varphi((X-a)^2+b^2+(f))=0$; that is, $(X-a)^2+b^2\in(f)$. Since this polynomial is monic and has the same degree as $f$, it must in fact be equal to $f$. Conversely, linear polynomials over a domain are irreducible by degree, and reducible quadratics have a root. A root of $f=(X-a)^2+b^2$ with $a,b\in R$ is an element $r\in R$ satisfying $(r-a)^2=-b^2$. If $b\neq0$, then dividing through would give a contradiction to the realness of $R$.Therefore $f$ must be irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: Classify $R[X]/(f)$ by the fundamental theorem; read off $f$ from the image of $X$, and check the converse directly.

nodes.name: Proof of Intermediate value property for polynomials
nodes.statement: We will prove that, for all $f\in R[X]$ and all $a,b\in R$ with $a\leq b$, if $f(a)\leq 0\leq f(b)$, then there is some $c\in[a,b]$ such that $f(c)=0$. Fix $a,b\in R$ with $a\leq b$, and proceed by induction on $\deg f$. If $\deg f=0$, then $f$ is constant and the result is clear. Otherwise, take a monic irreducible factor $g$ of $f$; then $g$ is classified by Lemma \ref{lem:irreds_class}. Observe that, if $g(a)$ and $g(b)$ are both positive, then $f/g$ satisfies the inductive hypothesis, and so has a root in $[a,b]$. If $g=(X-a)^2+b^2$ with $a,b\in R$ and $b\neq0$, then $g$ is everywhere positive. If $g=X-c$ with $c\in R$, then either $c\in[a,b]$ and $g(c)=0$, or $c\notin[a,b]$ and $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have the same sign. In this last case, either $f/g$ or $f/(-g)$ satsifies the inductive hypothesis. In all cases, $f$ has a root in $[a,b]$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $\deg f$, factoring off a monic irreducible factor classified by the previous lemma and checking its sign on $[a,b]$.

nodes.name: Proof of Intermediate value property implies real closed
nodes.statement: We use Lemma \ref{lem:RCF_ord_ax}. Let $a\in R$ be non-negative, and consider the polynomial $f=X^2-a$. Then $f(0)=-a\leq0$, but $f(a+1)=a^2+a+1>0$. By the intermediate value property, $f$ has a root in $R$, and so $a$ is a square in $R$. Let $f$ be an odd-degree polynomial over $R$. Write $f=a_nX^n+\cdots+a_0$. We will show $f$ has a root in $R$. Replacing $f$ by $-f$ if necessary, we may assume $a_n>0$. For $x>1$, we compute \[f(x)\geq x^{n-1}(a_nx-n\max_i|a_i|).\] Therefore, when $x>\max\{1,n\max_i|a_i|/a_n\}$, $f(x)>0$. A similar calculation shows that $f(x)<0$ for sufficiently large negative values of $x$. We are done by the intermediate value property.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the order axioms: IVP on $X^2-a$ gives square roots; bounding an odd polynomial at large $|x|$ gives a sign change.

By induction on degree, it suffices to show that irreducible odd-degree polynomials over $R$ are all linear. Let $f\in R[X]$ be such a polynomial, and consider the odd-degree field extension $R_f=R[X]/(f)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:ext_ord_odd_deg}, there is an ordering making $R_f/R$ an ordered extension. Therefore $\deg f=[R_f:R]=1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Index-2 real closed subfield of an algebraically closed field
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0. Observe that the prime subfield $\Q$ can be ordered. Further, given an ordered subfield $F$ with $\bar{F}\neq C$, we can use Lemma \ref{lem:order_fun_field} to adjoin an element transcendental over $F$, obtaining a strictly bigger ordered subfield. Apply Zorn's lemma to obtain a maximal ordered subfield $R\subseteq C$; then $\bar{R}=C$. By Theorem \ref{thm:ord_max_imp_RCF}, $R$ must be real closed. By Corollary \ref{cor:RCF_ac}, $C\cong R(i)$, and so $[C:R]=2$.

Therefore define $\varphi:K\to R$ with $\varphi(\alpha)=\beta$.

nodes.name: Proof of Unique order-preserving embedding into a real closure
nodes.statement: Fix a real closure $R'$ of $K$ (one exists by Lemma \ref{lem:real_closure_exists}). By the primitive element theorem, $K=F(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha\in K$. Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$, and let $\alpha_1<\cdots<\alpha_m$ be the roots of $f$ in $R'$, with $\alpha=\alpha_k$. By Theorem \ref{thm:Sturm}, $f$ also has $m$ roots in $R$; let them be $\beta_1<\cdots<\beta_m$. Since non-negative elements of $R'$ are squares, and $x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}\in R'$ such that $\alpha_{j+1}-\alpha_j=x_j^2$, and let $L=K(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m,r,x_1,\dots,x_{m-1})\leq R'$. Now, suppose we have a $K$-homomorphism $\psi:L\to R$. Each $\psi(\alpha_j)$ is equal to a different $\beta_i$. Then $\psi(\alpha_{j+1})-\psi(\alpha_j)=\psi(x_j)^2\geq0$, so $\psi(\alpha_1)<\cdots<\psi(\alpha_m)$, and so $\psi(\alpha_j)=\beta_j$ for all $j$. By Lemma \ref{lem:closure_emb_ext_unordered}, there is in fact an $F$-homomorphism $\varphi:L\to R$. We will show that $\varphi$ is order-preserving. Indeed, fix a non-negative element $x\in L$. As before, find $r\in R'$ such that $x=r^2$, and let $M=L(r)\leq R'$. Apply Lemma \ref{lem:closure_emb_ext_unordered} again to obtain an $L$-homomorphism $\psi:M\to R$; then $\varphi(x)=\psi(x)=\psi(r)^2\geq0$. Therefore $\varphi$ maps non-negative elements to non-negative elements, and so is order-preserving. Then $\varphi|_K$ is the map we want. Note that $\varphi(\alpha)=\beta_k$. To see uniqueness, let $\tilde\varphi:K\to R$ be an order-preserving $F$-homomorphism; by existence, $\tilde\varphi$ extends to a an order-preserving $K$-homomorphism $\tilde\psi:L\to R$. Then $\tilde\varphi(\alpha)=\tilde\psi(\alpha_k)=\beta_k=\varphi(\alpha)$, and so $\tilde\varphi=\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Adjoin square roots of root gaps so any homomorphism preserves the root order. Existence via the unordered embedding lemma, uniqueness by matching $\alpha=\alpha_k$ to $\beta_k$.

nodes.name: Fix a real closure $R'$ of $K$
nodes.statement: Fix a real closure $R'$ of $K$ (one exists by Lemma \ref{lem:real_closure_exists}).
nodes.statement_short: Fix a real closure $R'$ of $K$

nodes.name: Order the roots and adjoin square roots of the gaps
nodes.statement: By the primitive element theorem, $K=F(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha\in K$. Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$, and let $\alpha_1<\cdots<\alpha_m$ be the roots of $f$ in $R'$, with $\alpha=\alpha_k$. By Theorem \ref{thm:Sturm}, $f$ also has $m$ roots in $R$; let them be $\beta_1<\cdots<\beta_m$. Since non-negative elements of $R'$ are squares, and $x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}\in R'$ such that $\alpha_{j+1}-\alpha_j=x_j^2$, and let $L=K(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m,r,x_1,\dots,x_{m-1})\leq R'$. Now, suppose we have a $K$-homomorphism $\psi:L\to R$. Each $\psi(\alpha_j)$ is equal to a different $\beta_i$. Then $\psi(\alpha_{j+1})-\psi(\alpha_j)=\psi(x_j)^2\geq0$, so $\psi(\alpha_1)<\cdots<\psi(\alpha_m)$, and so $\psi(\alpha_j)=\beta_j$ for all $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Order the roots and adjoin square roots of the gaps

nodes.name: Existence of an order-preserving embedding
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:closure_emb_ext_unordered}, there is in fact an $F$-homomorphism $\varphi:L\to R$. We will show that $\varphi$ is order-preserving. Indeed, fix a non-negative element $x\in L$. As before, find $r\in R'$ such that $x=r^2$, and let $M=L(r)\leq R'$. Apply Lemma \ref{lem:closure_emb_ext_unordered} again to obtain an $L$-homomorphism $\psi:M\to R$; then $\varphi(x)=\psi(x)=\psi(r)^2\geq0$. Therefore $\varphi$ maps non-negative elements to non-negative elements, and so is order-preserving. Then $\varphi|_K$ is the map we want. Note that $\varphi(\alpha)=\beta_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Existence of an order-preserving embedding

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: To see uniqueness, let $\tilde\varphi:K\to R$ be an order-preserving $F$-homomorphism; by existence, $\tilde\varphi$ extends to a an order-preserving $K$-homomorphism $\tilde\psi:L\to R$. Then $\tilde\varphi(\alpha)=\tilde\psi(\alpha_k)=\beta_k=\varphi(\alpha)$, and so $\tilde\varphi=\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness

nodes.name: Proof of Uniqueness of the real closure
nodes.statement: Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be real closures of $F$. Applying Zorn's lemma to the set of ordered extensions intermediate between $R_1$ and $F$ having a unique order-preserving $F$-embedding into $R_2$, and using Lemma \ref{lem:closure_emb_ext}, we obtain an intermediate extension $R_1/K/F$ with no nontrivial finite ordered extensions and a unique order-preserving $F$-embedding $\varphi:K\to R_2$. If the ordered algebraic extension $R_2/\varphi(K)$ were nontrivial, then it would contain a nontrivial ordered finite extension, so $\varphi$ must be surjective (and so an $F$-isomorphism). In particular, $K\subseteq R_1$ is real closed; by maximality (Lemma \ref{lem:RCF_max}), in fact $K=R_1$ and so $\varphi$ is an $F$-isomorphism between $R_1$ and $R_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Zorn's lemma on partial embeddings with the unique-embedding lemma; maximality of real closed fields forces an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal partial embedding
nodes.statement: Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be real closures of $F$. Applying Zorn's lemma to the set of ordered extensions intermediate between $R_1$ and $F$ having a unique order-preserving $F$-embedding into $R_2$, and using Lemma \ref{lem:closure_emb_ext}, we obtain an intermediate extension $R_1/K/F$ with no nontrivial finite ordered extensions and a unique order-preserving $F$-embedding $\varphi:K\to R_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal partial embedding

nodes.name: $\varphi$ must be surjective
nodes.statement: If the ordered algebraic extension $R_2/\varphi(K)$ were nontrivial, then it would contain a nontrivial ordered finite extension, so $\varphi$ must be surjective (and so an $F$-isomorphism).
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi$ must be surjective

nodes.name: Maximality gives $K=R_1$
nodes.statement: In particular, $K\subseteq R_1$ is real closed; by maximality (Lemma \ref{lem:RCF_max}), in fact $K=R_1$ and so $\varphi$ is an $F$-isomorphism between $R_1$ and $R_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximality gives $K=R_1$

nodes.name: Proof of Real closed fields have no nontrivial automorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a real closed field. By Theorem \ref{thm:real_closure_unique}, $R$ has no nontrivial order-preserving automorphisms. Since the ordering on $R$ is unique (by Lemma \ref{lem:RCF_ord_unique}), every automorphism of $R$ must be order-preserving.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of real closure rules out order-preserving automorphisms; uniqueness of the order makes every automorphism order-preserving.

nodes.name: No nontrivial order-preserving automorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a real closed field. By Theorem \ref{thm:real_closure_unique}, $R$ has no nontrivial order-preserving automorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: No nontrivial order-preserving automorphisms

nodes.name: Every automorphism preserves the order
nodes.statement: Since the ordering on $R$ is unique (by Lemma \ref{lem:RCF_ord_unique}), every automorphism of $R$ must be order-preserving.
nodes.statement_short: Every automorphism preserves the order

nodes.name: Proof of Orderings of algebraic extensions correspond to embeddings
nodes.statement: Fix an ordering on $K$ extending that on $F$, and let $K$ have real closure $R_K$ (exists by Lemma \ref{lem:real_closure_exists}). Then $R_K/F$ is algebraic, so $R_K$ is a real closure of $F$. By Theorem \ref{thm:real_closure_unique}, there is an $F$-isomorphism to $R_K\cong R$, and this induces an $F$-homomorphism $K\to R$. Restricting the order on $R$ to $K$ via this map recovers the original order on $K$ by construction. Moreover, the inverse to order restriction constructed above is unique. Indeed, an inverse $\varphi:K\to R$ is order-preserving by definition, so it is an order-embedding from $K$ into its real closure. By Theorem \ref{thm:real_closure_unique}, such a map is unique.
nodes.statement_short: Embed $K$ into $R$ via a real closure of $K$ and uniqueness of real closures; the inverse is unique by uniqueness of the order-embedding.

nodes.name: Construct an embedding from an ordering
nodes.statement: Fix an ordering on $K$ extending that on $F$, and let $K$ have real closure $R_K$ (exists by Lemma \ref{lem:real_closure_exists}). nodes.name: The inverse is unique

nodes.statement_short: The inverse is unique

nodes.name: Proof of Weak Artin-Schreier theorem
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:FTAlg_converse_alg_closure}, it suffices to show that $\bar{R}\cong R(i)$. Since $\ch\bar{R}\neq 2$, we have $\bar{R}\cong R(\sqrt{a})$ for some non-square $a\in R$. Since $R(\sqrt{a})$ is algebraically closed, $\sqrt{a}$ is a square in $R(\sqrt{a})$; find $x,y\in R$ such that $\sqrt{a}=(x+y\sqrt{a})^2$. Expanding and comparing coefficients, $x^2+y^2a=0$ and $2xy=1$. Rearranging, $a=-(4x^4)=-1\cdot(2x^2)^2$. Rescaling by $2x^2$, $R(i)\cong R(\sqrt{a})=\bar{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\bar R\cong R(i)$; write $\bar R=R(\sqrt a)$, take a square root of $\sqrt a$ and compare coefficients to show $-a$ is a square.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\bar R\cong R(i)$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:FTAlg_converse_alg_closure}, it suffices to show that $\bar{R}\cong R(i)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\bar R\cong R(i)$

nodes.name: Compare coefficients to show $-a$ is a square

nodes.name: Proof of No finite-index subfields in nonzero characteristic
nodes.statement: Ordered fields have characteristic 0.
nodes.statement_short: Real closed fields are ordered, hence of characteristic 0; apply Artin-Schreier.

nodes.name: Proof of Finite-index subfields of the algebraic numbers
nodes.statement: Since $\Q_{\text{alg}}(i)=\bar{\Q}$, the field $\Q_{\text{alg}}$ is a finite-index subfield. By Theorem \ref{thm:Artin-Schreier}, any finite-index subfield has a unique ordering making it real closed. Let $R$ be a real closed subfield. Then the ordering on $R$ restricts to the ordering on $\Q$ (unique by Corollary \ref{cor:unique_ord_Q}). Since $R/\Q$ is algebraic, $R$ is a real closure of $\Q$. By Theorem \ref{thm:real_closure_unique}, there is a unique $\Q$-isomorphism $\psi:\Q_{\text{alg}}\cong R$. Since $\Q_{\text{alg}}(i)=R(i)=\bar{\Q}$, $\psi$ extends uniquely to $\varphi\in\Gal(\Q_{alg}/\Q(i))$ by mapping $i\to i$. The subfield $R$ is then recovered from $\varphi\in\Gal(\Q_{alg}/\Q(i))$ by taking $\varphi^{-1}(\Q_{\text{alg}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Artin-Schreier makes every finite-index subfield real closed, hence a real closure of $\Q$; uniqueness of real closures gives the parametrisation by Galois elements.

nodes.name: $\Q_{alg}$ has finite index
nodes.statement: Since $\Q_{\text{alg}}(i)=\bar{\Q}$, the field $\Q_{\text{alg}}$ is a finite-index subfield.

nodes.name: Each such subfield is a real closure of $\Q$, parametrised by $\Gal$

nodes.name: Both values of $g$ positive: induct on $f/g$
nodes.statement: Observe that, if $g(a)$ and $g(b)$ are both positive, then $f/g$ satisfies the inductive hypothesis, and so has a root in $[a,b]$.
nodes.statement_short: Both values of $g$ positive: induct on $f/g$

nodes.name: Quadratic $g$ is positive
nodes.statement: If $g=(X-a)^2+b^2$ with $a,b\in R$ and $b\neq0$, then $g$ is everywhere positive.
nodes.statement_short: Quadratic $g$ is positive

nodes.name: Linear $g$: root in interval or induct
nodes.statement: If $g=X-c$ with $c\in R$, then either $c\in[a,b]$ and $g(c)=0$, or $c\notin[a,b]$ and $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have the same sign. In this last case, either $f/g$ or $f/(-g)$ satsifies the inductive hypothesis.
nodes.statement_short: Linear $g$: root in interval or induct

nodes.name: Conclude in all cases
nodes.statement: In all cases, $f$ has a root in $[a,b]$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude in all cases
